## Adapting Tourism: From Skiing to Birdwatching

At the offices of Cetursa, the public company that manages the Sierra Nevada ski resort, snowfall records tell a story that is no longer up for debate. Since the year 2000, the ski season has lost an average of twenty usable days per year, a figure that forces a rethinking of the economic model for the entire southern slope of the mountain range. The resort, located about thirty kilometers from Capileira, remains a first-order tourist engine, but managers know that snow is no longer as reliable a resource as it was for the previous generation. Artificial snow cannons have cushioned part of the blow, although energy costs and water availability limit their responsiveness to increasingly shorter and milder winters.

This uncertainty has driven entrepreneurs in the Alpujarra to seek alternatives that do not depend on the weather forecast. The rural hotels in the region, accustomed to filling their rooms with skiers who preferred to sleep in the white villages rather than at the resort itself, have begun to market what they call extreme climate routes. The proposal consists of turning adversity into an attraction: hikes along slopes where the thaw exposes ancient snowfields, ascents to peaks that a decade ago remained snow-covered well into June, or walks along irrigation channels that in the depths of winter show an unusually generous flow. The visitor is no longer looking just for snow, but for the experience of a landscape undergoing accelerated transformation.

Birdwatching has become one of the cornerstones of this transition. Ornithological guides working on the southern slope of Sierra Nevada have documented in recent years an altitudinal shift in several emblematic species. The alpine accentor, a discreet bird that nests among rocky outcrops and scree, now appears at higher elevations than those recorded in the field guides of the 1990s. The snow finch, a symbol of the high Sierra Nevada mountains, follows a similar pattern: specimens that were once found at 2,500 meters are now more frequently observed above 2,800 meters, in search of the cool temperatures their physiology demands. The Sociedad Española de Ornitología, through its Andalusian delegation, has confirmed this trend in its periodic censuses.

For local guides, this movement of birds is not just a scientific fact: it is a business opportunity. Ornithological routes that were once concentrated in spring and autumn now extend throughout the year, because the behavior of the species has stopped conforming to classic seasonal patterns. A guide can offer an alpine accentor observation day in the middle of February in areas that traditionally remained inaccessible due to snow. The client, in turn, receives a narrative that goes beyond the simple identification of species: they are explained why that bird is where it is, what its presence at that altitude means, and how it relates to the changes the mountain range is experiencing. Nature becomes an outdoor classroom where global warming is observed through binoculars.

Rural accommodations have been quick to read this emerging demand. Several establishments in Capileira, Bubión, and Pampaneira offer packages that combine two or three nights' stay with guided birdwatching outings and interpretive climate routes. The chosen name, extreme climate routes, plays deliberately with ambiguity: these are not high-risk activities, but itineraries that show the visible effects of change in mountain ecosystems. The tourist who arrives looking for a quiet getaway finds a proposal that appeals to their intellectual curiosity, and occupancy data suggest that the formula works. On winter weekends, when the ski resort cannot guarantee enough snow, these packages maintain an acceptable level of bookings.

The transition is not without its tensions. Entrepreneurs most dependent on snow tourism watch with suspicion as public funds and institutional promotion begin to shift towards other segments. Mountain guides, for their part, have had to expand their training: it is no longer enough to know the techniques for moving across snowy terrain; there is now also a demand for the ability to interpret the landscape, identify species, and explain complex ecological processes. The Asociación de Guías de Sierra Nevada has incorporated modules on ornithology and climatology into its professional retraining programs, aware that the client profile is changing as fast as the climate itself.

The ski resort, far from being left on the sidelines, has begun to diversify its summer offerings. The lifts that transport skiers in winter also operate in summer to bring visitors to the high areas where the most interesting birds congregate. Cetursa has signed agreements with ornithological tourism companies to offer combined tickets that include cable car access and a guided tour. The infrastructure designed for skiing is thus repurposed to serve a nature tourism that does not depend on snow, a strategic shift that many consider inevitable. The twenty lost ski days since the year 2000 are not coming back, and the region knows it.

The result is a tourist destination that reinvents itself without giving up its identity. The Alpujarra remains the land of white villages, irrigation channels, and conical chimneys, but now it incorporates a new narrative: that of adaptation. Visitors drawn by skiing discover a territory that speaks to them of birds moving up the mountain, of disappearing snowfields, and of a local economy learning to move with the thermometer. Birdwatching, a niche activity just a decade ago, has become a pillar of the tourist offering on the southern slope of Sierra Nevada. And the guides who once cursed the lack of snow now rise early with their binoculars to show clients an alpine accentor perched on a rock that, not so long ago, remained covered by a meter of ice.
